paragraphs: UniAD addresses anomaly detection across several object categories using one model. This setting exposes a weakness in reconstruction approaches: a network may reproduce unusual inputs just as successfully as normal ones. If both are reconstructed well, reconstruction quality stops being useful for distinguishing anomalies. The paper calls this failure an identical shortcut.

The authors introduce three changes to discourage that shortcut. A decoder with query embeddings at each layer helps represent the distribution across categories. Neighbor masked attention restricts information passing directly from input features into their reconstructed counterparts. Feature jittering adds noise to the inputs and asks the model to recover the correct information, encouraging recovery beyond straightforward copying.

Experiments on MVTec-AD and CIFAR-10 report improvements over the evaluated alternatives. For a single model covering 15 MVTec-AD categories, the reported detection result increases from 88.1% to 96.5%, and localization from 89.5% to 96.8%, relative to the second competitor. These findings support the combination of shared modeling and measures that prevent reconstruction shortcuts.
neurips-2022-a-unified-model-for-multi-c.tldr: UniAD detects anomalies across multiple object categories with one reconstruction model designed to resist copying anomalous inputs.

paragraphs: This paper studies related classification tasks that share a label space but lack complete training coverage of the categories encountered at test time. A task may therefore need to recognize a category for which its own training data are missing. The proposed approach transfers relevant category knowledge from other tasks learned alongside it.

The method builds an association graph containing three kinds of nodes: tasks, classes, and individual examples. Edges encode their relationships, and message passing moves information among them. This gives each example access to categorical information beyond its immediate task, with the aim of making examples from different categories easier to distinguish.

To discourage misleading associations between tasks and classes, the authors maximize an assignment entropy that encourages class nodes to balance their edge weights. This is intended to make information from related tasks more broadly usable. Evaluations on three general benchmarks and a skin lesion classification dataset consistently outperform representative baselines. The results support explicitly modeling relationships among tasks, categories, and examples when category coverage changes between training and testing.
neurips-2022-association-graph-learning-.tldr: An association graph transfers category knowledge across related tasks to improve classification when individual tasks lack training examples for some test categories.

paragraphs: Standard reinforcement learning optimizes a scalar reward. Convex reinforcement learning broadens the formulation to objectives that are convex functions of the distribution of states visited by a policy. This includes applications such as imitation learning, risk-averse learning, and pure exploration, where the objective can depend on more than accumulated scalar rewards.

The paper examines a distinction between the state distribution associated with indefinitely many trials and the empirical visitation frequencies obtained from finitely many trajectories. In the classic formulation, optimizing these two versions leads to the same optimal policy. That equivalence makes the infinite-trials objective a theoretically sound substitute despite the finite amount of interaction available in practice.

The authors prove that this equivalence does not generally carry over to convex reinforcement learning. Substituting the infinite-trials objective for the finite-trials objective can produce a significant approximation error. The consequence concerns which problem an algorithm actually solves: a policy optimized for the distribution-level formulation may be poorly matched to the intended finite-trial objective. The paper argues that this distinction should inform methods and evaluation in convex reinforcement learning.
neurips-2022-challenging-common-assumpti.tldr: The paper proves that optimizing an infinite-trials objective can introduce significant error when the intended convex reinforcement learning objective involves finitely many trials.

paragraphs: ComGAN is an unsupervised generative model that produces realistic images together with semantically meaningful masks. Its training uses an adversarial loss and binary regularization. The paper examines why compositional generation can settle into two kinds of trivial solutions, identifying vanishing mask gradients as their source: the mask receives too little learning signal to develop the intended structure.

The authors address these failures through the network architecture. They then build DS-ComGAN, which contains two fully unsupervised modules. Its disentanglement module associates foreground, background, and mask with three independent variables, giving these image components separate representations. Its segmentation module learns to identify object regions.

The experiments report that the architectural design avoids the studied trivial solutions without supervised information or regularization for that purpose. DS-ComGAN also substantially outperforms the evaluated semi-supervised and weakly supervised methods on image disentanglement and unsupervised segmentation. Together, the findings suggest that improving how a generator composes images can help it learn useful object structure. The authors present this redesign as a possible direction for further unsupervised learning research.
neurips-2022-comgan-unsupervised-disenta.tldr: ComGAN uses architectural changes to avoid trivial compositional solutions and supports unsupervised learning of separate image components and object masks.

paragraphs: The paper studies zero-shot transfer between reinforcement learning tasks with different reward functions. In the successor features framework, generalized policy improvement uses information learned on source tasks to select behavior for a new target task. Existing transfer approaches rely on those source features or on additional predictions produced by a function approximator when given unfamiliar inputs.

The authors seek to improve transfer by controlling errors in the values predicted for the target task. They derive lower and upper bounds on optimal values for new task vectors that can be expressed as linear combinations of source task vectors. That expressibility condition identifies the class of new tasks covered by the stated bounds.

These bounds motivate constrained generalized policy improvement, a test-time method that constrains action-value approximation errors. Experiments in Scavenger and Reacher use state observations, while experiments in DeepMind Lab use visual observations. The method significantly improves transfer over prior generalized policy improvement in these evaluations. The contribution connects theoretical value bounds with a practical adjustment at transfer time, making source-task knowledge more useful for choosing actions on new tasks.
neurips-2022-constrained-gpi-for-zero-sh.tldr: Constrained GPI uses bounds derived from source tasks to improve zero-shot transfer by restricting target-task value approximation errors.

paragraphs: The paper investigates deepfake detection through local image details and how those details change over time. Earlier work had identified both as useful for generalizing across forgery methods, while still experiencing robustness problems after videos undergo post-processing. The proposed LTTD framework emphasizes temporal information within small spatial regions before forming a global decision.

Its Local Sequence Transformer models temporal consistency in sequences restricted to particular image regions. Shallow layers of learned three-dimensional filters progressively enhance low-level information in those sequences. This produces local temporal embeddings: representations that combine information about a small region with information about its behavior across time.

The framework then uses those embeddings for final classification through a global contrastive approach. This local-to-global organization lets the detector build its overall judgment from localized temporal evidence. Extensive experiments on popular datasets show that the method identifies local forgery cues and achieves state-of-the-art performance. The stated findings support focusing temporal modeling on restricted regions as a useful design choice for deepfake detection.
neurips-2022-delving-into-sequential-pat.tldr: LTTD detects deepfakes by modeling temporal consistency within local video regions and combining those representations into a global classification.

paragraphs: This paper introduces a differentiable framework for analog quantum computing. The adjustable parameters are defined at the level of analog control signals, or pulses. The aim is to make variational methods better exploit near-term quantum devices by optimizing this signal-level description of the computation.

A central technical contribution concerns obtaining gradients of quantum dynamics. The authors propose a scalable estimator that uses a forward pass together with Monte Carlo sampling. Those estimated gradients lead to a quantum stochastic gradient descent algorithm for training the framework. This connects the choice of pulse parameters with a procedure for updating them, making gradient-based optimization part of the proposed analog computing approach.

The authors apply the framework to quantum optimization and control and report an advantage of orders of magnitude over state-of-the-art approaches based on parameterized digital quantum circuits. This is an observed result for the studied applications. The contribution combines pulse-level parameterization with a scalable gradient estimation method, providing both a way to represent the computation and a way to train it.
neurips-2022-differentiable-analog-quant.tldr: A pulse-level analog quantum computing framework uses sampled gradient estimates and reports orders-of-magnitude advantages in studied optimization and control applications.

paragraphs: The paper asks whether strong object tracking must depend on Transformers, whose advances have accompanied larger training datasets and longer training periods. It proposes a convolutional approach that draws strength from combining vision and language. The central claim is that multimodal representations can make convolutional trackers competitive with, and sometimes better than, leading Transformer trackers.

The method learns unified, adaptive vision-language representations using a modality mixer called ModaMixer and an asymmetrical search over convolutional networks. These components make the interaction between visual and language information central to the tracking design. The authors also provide theoretical analysis supporting the effectiveness of their approach.

On LaSOT, the method raises a CNN-based Siamese tracker's SUC result from 50.7% to 65.2%, an increase of 14.5 percentage points. It also surpasses several Transformer-based state-of-the-art trackers. The authors describe their convolutional solution as more economical, and the results demonstrate a strong alternative within the evaluated setting. Their broader proposal is to give vision-language representation learning greater attention when designing future trackers.
neurips-2022-divert-more-attention-to-vi.tldr: Combining vision and language through ModaMixer and convolutional architecture search produces a tracker that outperforms several Transformer-based alternatives.

paragraphs: Boolean matrix factorization represents a Boolean input matrix using lower-rank Boolean factors combined through Boolean algebra. This can produce interpretable structure where ordinary nonnegative matrix factorization has interpretability difficulties on Boolean data. The obstacle is computational: finding the factors involves an NP-hard combinatorial optimization problem.

The authors reduce the practical burden by replacing the discrete formulation with a continuous relaxation. A new elastic-binary regularizer encourages the relaxed solution toward the intended binary structure. From this formulation, they derive a proximal gradient algorithm. The approach therefore connects a continuous optimization procedure with the goal of obtaining interpretable Boolean factors.

Experiments on synthetic data show rapid convergence, precise recovery of the underlying factors, and exact estimation of the simulated rank. On real-world data, the method improves on the evaluated state of the art in recall, loss, and runtime. A medical case study also finds the resulting factors interpretable and semantically meaningful. These are practical experimental successes for the proposed relaxation, supporting its usefulness for reducing the computational cost of Boolean factorization.
neurips-2022-efficiently-factorizing-boo.tldr: A continuous relaxation with an elastic-binary regularizer makes Boolean matrix factorization faster in experiments while retaining interpretable factors.

paragraphs: EvenNet addresses graph neural networks whose performance deteriorates when the tendency of connected nodes to share labels changes between training and testing. This tendency is called homophily; heterophilic graphs instead connect dissimilar nodes more often. Sensitivity to these changes can limit transfer between graphs and leave models vulnerable to attacks that alter graph structure.

The proposed model uses an even-polynomial graph filter in the spectral domain. Its defining restriction omits odd-hop neighbor contributions. The authors analyze the design in both spatial and spectral terms and show advantages over full-order models when generalizing across homophilic and heterophilic graphs. This provides theoretical support for using a restricted filter to improve robustness.

Experiments on synthetic and real-world datasets support the approach. EvenNet outperforms existing defense models against structural attacks without adding computational costs, while remaining competitive on conventional node classification tasks across both graph types. The findings make a case for addressing this robustness problem through the model's filter structure, offering a simple design alongside defenses that learn new graph structures or calculate edge attention.
neurips-2022-evennet-ignoring-odd-hop-ne.tldr: EvenNet restricts graph filtering to even-order terms to improve robustness to homophily changes and structural attacks.

paragraphs: Removing rain from an image requires distinguishing rain streaks from object texture, even when they look similar. Misclassifying pixels can leave rain behind or erase useful detail. SEIDNet addresses this ambiguity by modeling possible rain-or-object statuses for individual pixels and then separating the corresponding appearance information.

Its status estimation component embeds pixel statuses in a space from which multiple possibilities can be sampled. This allows the model to represent a pixel's ambiguous interpretation. The information decoupling component uses those statuses to separate rain appearance from object appearance. It then constructs a kernel space, sampling multiple kernels for each pixel to remove rain and recover the object's appearance.

Evaluations on public datasets report state-of-the-art rain removal performance. Additional experiments show that the approach can be extended to other restoration tasks, including snow, haze, and shadow removal, with state-of-the-art results. The findings support treating ambiguous pixel identity explicitly and using that information to guide restoration, so the model can address both unwanted weather effects and preservation of scene details.
neurips-2022-generative-status-estimatio.tldr: SEIDNet samples possible pixel identities and restoration kernels to separate rain from object detail, with strong results across several restoration tasks.

paragraphs: Self-training uses predictions on unlabeled examples as training targets. A common implementation relies on a momentum teacher updated from past student models. Incorrect predictions can then become incorrect supervision and accumulate, producing confirmation bias. This paper attributes that problem primarily to using a teacher built from earlier student knowledge to guide the current student.

Future-self-training changes the order of operations. At each step, it virtually optimizes the student by caching gradients without applying them to the current model weights. It updates the teacher using this virtual future student, then asks that teacher to generate pseudo-labels for the current student. The teacher's guidance therefore incorporates a prospective update.

The authors also introduce FST-D and FST-W, variants that explore the future more deeply and more widely. Experiments cover unsupervised domain adaptive semantic segmentation and semi-supervised semantic segmentation across a broad range of settings. They report improved pseudo-label quality and segmentation performance. The results support changing when teacher information is formed as a useful way to alleviate the self-reinforcement of prediction errors.
neurips-2022-learning-from-future-a-nove.tldr: Future-self-training uses a virtual student update to improve teacher-generated pseudo-labels and alleviate confirmation bias in semantic segmentation.

paragraphs: This paper studies least-squares learning from dependent time-series data. Many existing bounds discount the effective number of samples by the process's mixing time, even after an initial burn-in period. The authors ask when dependence can be accommodated without that continuing penalty in the order of the learning rate.

Their main result assumes a realizable setting, martingale difference noise, and a trajectory hypercontractivity condition. Under these conditions, the least-squares estimator's excess risk matches the independent-data rate in order after burn-in. The permitted covariate processes can retain long-range correlations under conditions substantially weaker than geometric ergodicity. The result therefore allows fast learning without requiring dependence to disappear rapidly.

The paper gives examples involving certain bounded function classes, finite-state irreducible and aperiodic Markov chains, parametric models, and infinite-dimensional ellipsoids. It also applies the theory to identifying nonlinear dynamics with generalized linear model transitions, obtaining a nearly minimax optimal excess risk bound after polynomial burn-in. These findings identify concrete conditions under which correlated observations remain statistically useful at essentially the independent-sample rate.
neurips-2022-learning-with-little-mixing.tldr: Under stated trajectory and noise conditions, least-squares learning from dependent time series matches the independent-data rate after burn-in.

paragraphs: Variational Bayesian inference often approximates a complicated posterior with a simpler distribution. Gaussian mean-field approximations make this tractable, but have been associated with underfitting in Bayesian neural networks with small datasets or large models. This paper identifies invariances in an overparameterized model's likelihood as one contributor to that behavior.

Likelihood invariances introduce discrete or continuous modes into the posterior that a Gaussian mean-field distribution cannot represent well. The authors show that this creates an additional gap in the evidence lower bound compared with a posterior designed to account for the invariances. Crucially, the gap changes with the approximation and disappears as it returns to the prior, connecting the objective's behavior to the underfitting phenomenon.

The analysis begins with translation invariance in a linear model containing one data point. There, the true posterior can be constructed from a mean-field parameterization, but only when the objective accounts for the invariance gap. The authors then extend their analysis to neural networks. The contribution is a framework for understanding this source of approximation error and investigating ways to address it.
neurips-2022-on-the-detrimental-effect-o.tldr: Likelihood invariances can worsen mean-field variational underfitting by creating a posterior approximation gap that vanishes as the approximation returns to the prior.

paragraphs: Choosing a recommender system requires deciding both which algorithm to use and how to configure it. This paper investigates why that decision remains labor intensive. Its large-scale study compares 24 algorithms and 100 hyperparameter sets across 85 datasets and 315 evaluation metrics, examining how performance changes with the data and the criterion used to judge success.

The study finds that the best algorithm and configuration depend strongly on the dataset and metric. It also finds strong correlations between algorithm performance and measurable characteristics of datasets. Those correlations motivate learning from previous recommendation problems to help choose a system for an unfamiliar one.

The resulting method, RecZilla, predicts an algorithm and hyperparameters for new datasets using meta-learning. The authors report that substantially more meta-training data than prior work helps reduce the human involvement required for new applications. They also release experimental results alongside code and pretrained models, allowing practitioners to train a selector for their preferred metric. The findings support making recommendation-system selection explicitly sensitive to both dataset characteristics and evaluation priorities.
neurips-2022-on-the-generalizability-and.tldr: RecZilla learns from a large comparison of recommendation algorithms to predict suitable algorithms and hyperparameters for new datasets and evaluation goals.

paragraphs: Optimal Brain Compression studies how to compress an already trained neural network without retraining it. The available information consists of the accurate model and a small set of calibration inputs. This is a demanding setting because compression must preserve useful behavior without a subsequent training stage to repair the model.

The framework handles both pruning, which removes weights, and quantization, which reduces their numerical precision. Its technical foundation is an exact, efficient realization of the classical Optimal Brain Surgeon framework, extended to quantization at the scale of modern deep networks. Bringing both operations into one framework also makes their combined use part of the same compression approach.

The authors report time and space efficiency together with significant improvements in the trade-off between compression and accuracy compared with existing post-training methods. Their experiments also show that pruning and quantization can be applied together accurately in this setting. These findings support a unified route to reducing model representation costs using limited calibration data, with potential execution benefits where software and hardware support the compressed formats.
neurips-2022-optimal-brain-compression-a.tldr: Optimal Brain Compression unifies pruning and quantization to improve compression–accuracy trade-offs without retraining, using only a small calibration dataset.

paragraphs: A conditional mean embedding represents the conditional distribution of an outcome given an input inside a reproducing kernel Hilbert space. It supports computing conditional expectations of functions in that space and has applications in nonparametric causal and Bayesian inference. This paper studies the consistency and learning rate of an estimator based on kernel ridge regression.

The analysis covers a misspecified setting in which the target embedding is a Hilbert–Schmidt operator from an input interpolation space into the target Hilbert space. The input space lies between the input kernel space and L2. The authors show that this operator space is equivalent, through an isomorphism, to a newly defined vector-valued interpolation space.

That connection enables an adaptive statistical learning rate for the empirical estimator. The analysis matches the optimal O(log n / n) rate without requiring the target Hilbert space to have finite dimension. A lower bound establishes optimality of the obtained upper bound. The contribution therefore gives both an error guarantee and evidence that its rate cannot generally be improved within the analyzed setting.
neurips-2022-optimal-rates-for-regulariz.tldr: The paper establishes optimal learning rates for regularized conditional mean embeddings in a misspecified setting without requiring a finite-dimensional target space.

paragraphs: Learning curves describe how prediction error changes as more training examples become available. This paper investigates kernel ridge regression in scaling regimes between familiar large-sample analyses and high-dimensional analyses where sample count grows linearly with dimension. It considers higher-order relationships in which the sample count grows like an integer power of dimension.

For dot-product kernels, the authors derive precise formulas for average test error, bias, and variance. Their setting assumes inputs drawn uniformly from a sphere and isotropic random labels. The asymptotic analysis lets the sample count grow while holding its ratio to the rth power of dimension constant, making each order of scaling a distinct regime to study.

The resulting learning curves have a peak near a sample count of d^r / r! for each integer order r. This produces multiple episodes of descent as the number of samples increases, with nontrivial behavior at several scales. Within the stated distributional and scaling assumptions, the formulas give a more detailed account of performance changes than a single linear relationship between sample count and dimension can provide.
neurips-2022-precise-learning-curves-and.tldr: Precise kernel regression formulas reveal repeated learning-curve peaks when sample counts scale as successive powers of input dimension.

paragraphs: This paper investigates how existing unsupervised object segmentation models behave on challenging real-world single images. Its contribution is a systematic empirical study. The motivating discrepancy is substantial: models can perform extremely well on simple synthetic datasets while failing severely to separate generic objects in real photographs.

The authors introduce four complexity factors that quantify appearance and geometry biases at both object and scene levels in datasets with human annotations. These factors provide a way to characterize differences between synthetic and real images. Experiments on multiple groups of ablated real-world datasets then investigate how those differences relate to segmentation failure.

The study identifies challenging distributions of object and scene appearance and geometry as key factors behind the failures. The assumptions built into the evaluated models have difficulty capturing this diversity, despite their success on simpler synthetic data. The findings suggest that future network designs should incorporate more explicit objectness biases. They also show why performance on simple synthetic scenes can give an incomplete picture of a model's ability to discover objects in real images.
neurips-2022-promising-or-elusive-unsupe.tldr: A systematic study links existing unsupervised segmentation models' real-image failures to appearance and geometry distributions poorly captured by their built-in biases.

paragraphs: Improving an image's visual quality does not necessarily help an object detector interpret it. The paper starts from reports that existing restoration methods sometimes leave detection performance unchanged or even reduce it. It therefore asks how restoration training can explicitly support detection under adverse imaging conditions.

The proposed pipeline uses a targeted adversarial attack during the restoration procedure. An ADAM-like attack generates pseudo ground truth for training the restoration model. The intended result is a restored image that stays close to the original sharp image while also producing better object detection results. This connects the supervision used for restoration with the needs of the downstream detector.

Experiments on dehazing and low-light enhancement show advantages over conventional training, domain adaptation methods, and multi-task methods. The authors state that the pipeline can be applied across restoration methods and to both one-stage and two-stage detectors. The findings support judging restoration partly through the task it is meant to enable: preserving a sharp appearance and helping a detector can be jointly addressed through the training targets.
neurips-2022-rethinking-image-restoratio.tldr: Attack-generated restoration targets help produce images that remain close to sharp originals while improving downstream object detection.

paragraphs: Many self-supervised methods create two transformed views of an example and learn from knowing that they belong together. This paper connects that practice to an efference copy: the brain's internal copy of a motor command that changes its environment. The proposed connection emphasizes that a copy of the command carries more information than a simple signal that two observations are related.

Self-supervision Through Efference Copies, or S-TEC, uses this perspective to build a common theoretical framework. It formally recovers and extends SimCLR, BYOL, and ReLIC. Its biological foundation also considers the likelihood that action representations are egocentric. The framework makes information about transformations central to the account of how useful sensory representations can be learned.

Experiments show meaningful changes to representations within and between classes, along with improvements to strong self-supervised baselines in image classification, segmentation, object detection, and audio. These findings support the machine-learning formulation. They also motivate a testable hypothesis that the brain's motor outputs positively influence its sensory representations; the reported computational results serve as motivation for that biological hypothesis.
neurips-2022-self-supervised-learning-th.tldr: S-TEC uses the neuroscience concept of efference copies to unify and extend self-supervised learning methods, with improvements across visual and audio tasks.

paragraphs: This paper examines small subnetworks called winning tickets as image recognizers when training data are scarce. The subnetworks are obtained through magnitude pruning under the lottery ticket hypothesis. The main empirical finding is that sparsity can accompany improved recognition: with 50–100 examples per class, these subnetworks substantially outperform their original dense networks.

The authors also combine winning tickets with data augmentation and with fine-tuning from a self-supervised backbone. These combinations produce further improvements, reaching as much as 16 percentage points on low-sample datasets and long-tailed classification. The results show that the benefits observed for sparse subnetworks can work alongside these additional approaches to learning from limited data.

Further experiments find greater robustness to synthetic noise and distribution shifts than in the dense counterparts. Analysis shows that the sparse networks retain relatively dense initial layers and learn more generalizable representations. Together, these observations support using winning tickets as data-efficient recognizers in the studied settings. The paper's evidence concerns their empirical recognition and robustness benefits as well as their reduced number of weights.
neurips-2022-sparse-winning-tickets-are-.tldr: Magnitude-pruned winning tickets outperform dense image networks in studied low-data settings and show improved robustness to noise and distribution shifts.

paragraphs: The paper explains a preference of stochastic gradient descent for flat minima through linear stability. It studies overparameterized models trained with square loss and measures sharpness using the Frobenius norm of the Hessian. This asks whether the local behavior of the optimization process permits it to remain near a particular global minimum.

The authors prove that a linearly stable global minimum must have sharpness bounded on the order of the square root of batch size divided by learning rate. Otherwise, SGD escapes exponentially fast. The bound does not depend on model size or sample size. It supplies a necessary condition for linear stability in the analyzed setting.

The explanation relies on SGD noise concentrating in sharp directions, with magnitude proportional to the loss. The authors prove this alignment property for linear networks and random feature models and verify it empirically for nonlinear networks. CIFAR-10 experiments further support the theory's practical relevance. The distinction between these theoretical and empirical findings matters: the paper provides a specific noise-based mechanism connecting stability with the selection of flatter minima.
neurips-2022-the-alignment-property-of-s.tldr: A stability analysis links SGD's preference for flat minima to noise aligned with sharp directions and derives a sharpness bound for stable global minima.

paragraphs: UnfoldML addresses prediction problems with ordered stages, where one stage precedes another. A single classifier trained across all stages and all available data can be expensive to deploy. The proposed pipeline separates that classifier into stage-specific classifiers, each using the data modalities or features needed for its own prediction.

Within each stage, classifiers form a cascade from cheaper to more expensive binary models. Cost and uncertainty guide dynamic prediction across stages and classifier complexity. This structure allows users to navigate the trade-off between accuracy and inference cost while also supporting early predictions of subsequent stages.

In clinical evaluations, UnfoldML stays within 0.1% accuracy of the best-performing multiclass baseline, saves close to 20 times the spatiotemporal inference cost, and predicts disease onset 3.5 hours earlier. An image classification application predicts labels at different levels, from coarse to fine, achieving nearly fivefold cost savings with as little as a 0.4% accuracy reduction. These findings support allocating prediction effort according to stage and uncertainty in the evaluated applications.
neurips-2022-unfoldml-cost-aware-and-unc.tldr: UnfoldML combines stage-specific classifier cascades with uncertainty-based decisions to reduce inference costs while preserving accuracy and enabling earlier predictions.

paragraphs: VAEL combines a variational autoencoder with probabilistic logic programming to create a neuro-symbolic generative model. Alongside ordinary latent variables, it includes a structured representation defined through a probabilistic logic program. That additional representation supports logical reasoning within the generative process, connecting learned neural information with explicitly structured knowledge.

The entire process is differentiable from end to end. After training, the model can address previously unseen generation tasks by reusing knowledge acquired in its neural component and applying new logical programs to the structured latent space. The design gives the learned representation and the logical program complementary roles in determining what the model generates.

Experiments provide support for benefits in both task generalization and data efficiency. The central result is evidence that this integration can help a generative model use acquired knowledge under new logical specifications. The authors describe the framework, to their knowledge, as the first general-purpose end-to-end integration of probabilistic logic programming into a deep generative model. Its contribution includes both that integrated architecture and the demonstrated benefits of combining its components.
neurips-2022-vael-bridging-variational-a.tldr: VAEL combines variational autoencoders with probabilistic logic so learned neural knowledge can support new generation tasks specified through logical programs.
